newsitem.title: GERMANY: Siemens ends IBIS trade down nine pct.
newsitem.headline: Siemens ends IBIS trade down nine pct.

text.p: Shares in German electronics company Siemens fell sharply on Wednesday to end electronic dealings down almost nine percent, after the firm said it saw no improvement in results for the 1996/97 financial year.

"Siemens is the absolute loser, everybody is giving up Siemens and buying everything else," said one dealer. Another trader said a "strong-sell" recommendation from a major U.S. investment house had helped push the stock down further.
Siemens shares dived over 9.5 percent from a day high of 80.70 marks ($53) to a low of 72.27 marks in heavy IBIS electronic trade, as over eleven million shares changed hands.
The stock had not been this low since late September last year, when it hit a low of 71.82 marks in IBIS dealings.

The shares, which had been named "stock of 1996" at the end of last year, recovered slightly to end computer dealings down 7.17 marks at 72.80 marks, as the whole market was buoyed by a firm opening on Wall Street.

The DAX index of 30 leading shares ended IBIS trade up 19.12 points, or 0.70 percent at 2735.28, but could have tested a record high at 2,745.82 points had it not been weighed down by Siemens, the index's fifth heaviest stock.

The company had earlier reported 1995/96 group net profit of 2.49 billion marks compared with 2.08 billion the previous year. But dealers said Siemens statement that said it saw no improvement in results for the 1996/97 financial year had prompted the sell-off.
"A catastrophe! The major disappointment is the forecast for this year," said analyst Hans Peter Wodniok at Credit Lyonnais in Frankfurt.
"The stock price will not have the potential to outperform the market for at least one year, until they have a positive surprise for us," he said.
Analysts had been forecasting earnings per share up at 5.80 marks, but Wodniok said those would now be scaled back to about 4.70 marks.

Dealers said they were particularly surprised about the company's forecast, because the 1996/97 financial year had only just begun. "How can one make a forecast, when the financial year has only just begun," said one trader.
